lessons.title: What College Really Costs
objectives: Compute cost of attendance and net price.
lessons.hook: Two schools: $31,000 and $68,000 sticker prices. Which is cheaper? Reveal aid offers.

notes.body: Tuition, fees, housing, food, books, transportation, personal.
Categorize every line: gift, earned, loan (and whose loan).

discussion: Why might the sticker price mislead families?
reflection: What questions would you ask a college’s financial aid office?
lessons.extension: Use a college’s net price calculator with a fictional family profile.
lessons.realWorld: Every college must post a net price calculator on its website.

lessons.title: Student Loans and Repayment
objectives: Calculate student-loan payments and total interest.
Explain subsidized vs. unsubsidized loans and capitalization.
lessons.hook: “I’ll worry about loans after graduation.” What could go wrong?

notes.body: Use the installment formula; standard federal plan is 10 years.
Unpaid interest added to principal increases future interest.
Payments around 10% of gross income or less are often considered manageable.

discussion: How might loan payments affect other life goals?
misconceptions: Discuss interest accrual and collection consequences.
reflection: What is the most you would be willing to borrow, and why?
lessons.extension: Research income-driven repayment plans on studentaid.gov.
lessons.realWorld: Federal loan rates are set each year; private loans vary by credit.

lessons.title: Comparing Career Earnings
objectives: Include forgone earnings and costs in comparisons.
lessons.hook: Graph: degree vs. apprenticeship cumulative earnings. Where do the lines cross?

notes.body: Earnings − education costs − loan payments over time.
Salaries vary by region, field, and person.

reflection: What matters to you in a career beyond pay?
lessons.extension: Use the Decision Lab “College & Career ROI Explorer”.

extend: Find the year when cumulative earnings cross.

lessons.realWorld: The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists median pay and outlook by occupation.

lessons.title: Payback and ROI of Education
lessons.hook: Claim: “College is always worth it.” Students sort evidence cards into support/refute.

notes.body: Completion rates, job placement, and debt load.
Interest and aptitude affect success and earnings.

discussion: Why might two students choose differently with the same data?
reflection: Which pathway are you considering, and what is its ROI?
lessons.extension: Research a real program’s completion rate on the College Scorecard.
lessons.realWorld: The federal College Scorecard reports costs, debt, and earnings by program.

solutionSteps: Community college → transfer: gain $24,000; payback $49,000 ÷ $24,000 ≈ 2 years.
4-year state university: gain $24,000; payback $78,000 ÷ $24,000 ≈ 3.3 years.
Electrician apprenticeship: gain $28,000; payback $3,000 ÷ $28,000 ≈ 0.1 years.
questions.modelResponse: The apprenticeship has the fastest payback (0.1 years) and the highest completion rate, so it is lowest-risk financially. The transfer path reaches the same degree outcome as the university for less money (payback 2 vs 3.3 years). The best choice depends on Mateo's interests and career goals; if Mateo wants a field that requires a degree, the transfer path offers the best value.
